catalog_quote: In this paper, I have shown that a single type of metrical foot structure is useful for characterizing both segmental and tonal processes in Medʉmba, a Grassfields Bantu language. Furthermore, I have shown that, despite the lack of stress in Medʉmba, heads of trochaic feet in the language display temporal properties consistent with metrical prominence found in stress-based languages such as English. This finding supports the notion that only a single type of metrical foot structure is necessary across languages, and that this structure can influence the phonology of both segments and tones.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (12 pp., XeTeX text, no scanned needed). The quoted passage is on p.11 under "6 Conclusion" exactly as given: "In this paper, I have shown that a single type of metrical foot structure is useful for characterizing both segmental and tonal processes in Medʉmba, a Grassfields Bantu language. Furthermore, I have shown that, despite the lack of stress in Medʉmba, heads of trochaic feet in the language display temporal properties consistent with metrical prominence found in stress-based languages such as English." (extracted text renders the ʉ glyph as "0"; otherwise word-for-word). Surrounding section read: §1 (p.1) frames African tone languages as "typically lack[ing] stress"; §2 (p.2)…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Medʉmba is a two-tone (H/L) language with no word stress. It does have word-level metrical prominence: stems are parsed into maximally disyllabic trochaic feet built from right to left and right-aligned with the prosodic word, so the foot head is the stem-initial syllable (the penult of a disyllabic stem, the first syllable of a monosyllabic one). Diagnostics: only the stem-initial syllable carries the full 48-consonant/11-vowel inventory (non-initial syllables have 7 consonants and only [ə]); stem-medial consonants lenite; falling contour tones are allowed only in foot-head position; in trisyllabic English loans a H tone is placed on the penult even where the source has no stress there; in speech-cycling experiments stem-initial syllables (not prefixes or stem-final syllables) align to harmonic phase positions like English stressed syllables.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not applicable (no stress). Franich 2021 (preprint p.32) notes that Medʉmba lacks 'hallmarks of a stress system, such . evidence for cyclic secondary stress' as a general point about such languages; feet are maximally disyllabic and multiple feet can be parsed in longer (loan) words, e.g. ká(bí.ndə̀) 'carpenter' (Franich 2014 p.112).
new_statements.exceptions: Pronominal enclitics behave like foot heads in speech cycling despite showing clitic-like lenition (Franich 2018 p.10; 2017 p.90-91; 2021 §5.1) — treated as a change in progress. Compounds are excluded from the foot generalizations (Franich 2014 fn.5). Echo vowels after glottal consonants in some verb roots are an apparent exception to V2 = schwa (Franich 2014 fn.5).
new_statements.domain_note: Word/stem level: prominence is defined on the prosodic word (stem plus affixes), with the foot head at the stem-initial syllable; elicited words and repeated short sentences (speech-cycling experiments, speakers from Bangangté/Bazou/Bangoulap). A separate phrase-level high preverbal phrase accent is described in Franich 2019/2021 Language and Speech. Speakers are from the Bangangté area (Bazou and Bangoulap dialects mentioned).
new_statements.identity_note: All Franich sources describe Medʉmba (Bamileke-Medumba, ISO byv, Glottolog medu1238) as spoken around Bangangté, Ndé division, Cameroon, with speakers from the Bazou and Bangoulap dialects noted; Voorhoeve's older work is labelled 'Bamileke (Bangangté dialect)', which is the same variety. No differently named variety is involved.

new_statements.quote: As mentioned, Medʉmba does not have clear evidence of lexical stress as measured through changes in amplitude or duration, but certain phonological patterns provide evidence for word-level prominence asymmetries in the language. [p. 4] ... In Medʉmba, stem-initial position is the strongest attractor of gestures, consistent with previous work which has argued for metrical prominence of stem-initial syllables (Franich 2018; 2021). [p. 27]

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the existing Franich 2018 AMP statement (no stress in Medʉmba, but metrical prominence asymmetries) and adds an independent line of evidence (gesture timing) that the prominent position is the stem-initial syllable, plus a note on enclitic (secondary-like) prominence from Franich 2021. Compatible with the trochaic-foot/stem-initial analysis in the previously checked Franich 2014/2017/2021 files. The catalog record itself has an empty rule; this work supports filling it with 'tonal; no lexical stress; stem-initial metrical prominence'.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Medʉmba is a tone language (underlying H vs L, p. 4) with no typical acoustic correlates of lexical stress (no increased duration or intensity, p. 3; no amplitude/duration cue, p. 4). Word-level metrical prominence nonetheless exists and falls on the stem-initial syllable: that position carries the full vowel and consonant contrasts while non-initial positions reduce to schwa and lenite (pp. 4-5), and co-speech gesture apexes are attracted to the stem-initial syllable (p. 27, p. 32). No individual tone value (H or L) is more prominent than the other (abstract p. 1; p. 32).
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 31: 'Franich (2021) finds that pronominal enclitics bear greater rhythmic prominence than stem-final syllables in Medʉmba (similar to the effects of secondary stress in English).' The paper itself treats prominence as binary and does not test gradient levels.
new_statements.exceptions: Stem-initial position is only a probabilistic 'default' attractor; 'there are clearly many cases where these sources were not sufficient to explain gesture timing' (p. 27). Phrase position matters: gestures are 'repelled' from phrase boundaries and realized later when a word follows a phrase boundary (p. 27). Word-initial vs stem-initial position did not reach significance as a separate predictor (p. 15). The Medʉmba data come from six speakers from the village of Bangoulap, Ndé Division, West Region (p. 10).
new_statements.identity_note: The 2025 Glossa study's Medʉmba speakers are from the village of Bangoulap, Ndé Division, West Region of Cameroon (p. 10); Franich's earlier work (dissertation p. 6, per the existing note) was on the Bangangté variety, also Ndé Division. The paper describes the language generally as 'a Grassfields Bantu language spoken in Cameroon by approximately 200,000 people' (p. 4) and cites Keupdjio 2021 and Voorhoeve 1971 for the same language. The Igbo half of the paper (Ọ̀nịchà and Owerri dialects) is not about Medʉmba.

tone_statements.citation: Franich, Kathryn & Hermann Keupdjio. 2022. The Influence of Tone on the Alignment of Speech and Co-Speech Gesture. In Proceedings of Speech Prosody 2022, Lisbon, 307-311. ISCA. doi:10.21437/SpeechProsody.2022-63
tone_statements.quote: Like many Bantu languages, Med0mba contrasts only level high (H) and low (L) tones, but contour tones can result where H and L tones associate to a single syllable. … Med0mba … contrasts only H and L tones, but allows contour tones in a variety of contexts. Some of these contours occur as the result of docking of segmentless floating tone morphemes to neighboring syllables. … HLH sequences (or HLLH sequences) in Med0mba typically result in lowering of the second H (HLŤH), and lowering of the register of all subsequent H and L tones within a clause.

tone_statements.summary: Two level tones, H and L; falling contours arise when H and L link to one syllable (e.g. via floating associative tone); automatic downstep HLꜜH lowers the register; no vowel-length contrast.

A prenasalized low verb has a different tone from its non-prenasalized counterpart.

tone_statements.citation: Franich, Kathryn H (2016). Internal and contextual cues to tone perception in Medumba. The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 140. ASA. pp. EL107–EL112.
tone_statements.quote: Specifically, we investigate the alignment of co-speech gestures in Med0mba, a Grassfields Bantu language spoken in Cameroon, in naturally-occurring conversational contexts. Similar to other Bantu languages, it has a two-tone system, with both high (H) and low (L) tones. Rising and falling ‘contour’ tones can also arise through a variety of morphological and syntactic processes (see [17] for further detail) but are reduceable to sequences of high + low (for falling) and low + high (for rising) (1).
tone_statements.locator: p. 307, sec. 1.2 'Gesture and f0 in a Tone Language' (right column), with Table 1 'Four tonal patterns found in Medʉmba'
tone_statements.summary: Two tones, high and low; rising and falling contours arise morphosyntactically and reduce to L+H and H+L; stem-initial prominence is independent of tone, with no canonical acoustic word-stress cues.

tone_statements.citation: Franich, Kathryn, Catherine O'Connor & Jonathan Barnes. 2012. Tonal merger in Medumba (Bamileke) nouns. Selected Proceedings of the 42nd Annual Conference on African Linguistics, 32-46. Cascadilla.
tone_statements.quote: Phonemically, Med umba has only a binary tonal contrast between high and low tones. Falling and rising tones can occur in many contexts, though they are analyzable, as in most other African tone languages, as sequences of level tones (Leben 1971; Goldsmith 1976; Clements and Goldsmith 1984). For example, verb stems carry one of two tone melodies, H or LH, and can be either monosyllabic or disyllabic. As can be seen in (4), monosyllabic verbs can host LH contours, while the LH melody is distributed as a sequence of two level tones on a disyllabic verb.
tone_statements.locator: p. 6, section 'Phonological and morphological structure in Medʉmba' > 'Tonal Structure'
tone_statements.summary: Two phonemic tones, high and low; rising/falling contours are LH/HL sequences, allowed only on stem-initial syllables; verb stems carry H or LH melodies; floating tones dock; tonal overwrite on verbs.

sources.note: Acoustic abstract: Medumba is tonal; the verbal nasal prefix is not a tone-bearing unit yet bears a high tone, realised as raised F0 on the following TBU. Only 'high' is named; no inventory stated.

tone.quote: anecdotal evidence suggests that the nasal prefix may be a non-TBU [Keupdjio 2018, PC] in which case it cannot bear a high tone. … Acoustic results show that the F0 contour of the nasal prefix itself is largely determined by the F0 trend of the preceding vowel, and no F0 change is observed at the onset of the nasal prefix, confirming that the verbal N-prefix is a non-TBU in Medumba. However, the nasal prefix appears to induce a raised F0 at the onset of the following TBU, indicating that, although the N-prefix itself does not express tone, it nevertheless “bears” a high tone.

tone.quote: In this paper, we examine whether the presence of a gesture can have an influence on timing of pitch peaks in Medʉmba, a tonal Grassfields Bantu language. Manual gesture data were analyzed from spontaneous interview speech of six Medʉmba speakers. … The findings did indicate, however, that f0 peaks—particularly for high, falling, and low tone syllables—were realized earlier in gesture-accompanied vowels than non gesture-accompanied vowels (p < .05).

tone.quote: Specifically, we investigate the alignment of co-speech gestures in Med0mba, a Grassfields Bantu language spoken in Cameroon, in naturally-occurring conversational contexts. Similar to other Bantu languages, it has a two-tone system, with both high (H) and low (L) tones. Rising and falling ‘contour’ tones can also arise through a variety of morphological and syntactic processes (see [17] for further detail) but are reduceable to sequences of high + low (for falling) and low + high (for rising) (1).
tone.locator: p. 307, sec. 1.2 'Gesture and f0 in a Tone Language' (right column), with Table 1 'Four tonal patterns found in Medʉmba'
tone.summary: Two tones, high and low; rising and falling contours arise morphosyntactically and reduce to L+H and H+L; stem-initial prominence is independent of tone, with no canonical acoustic word-stress cues.
